standard.title: Inclusive and exclusive language effects
standard.description: understand how language can have inclusive and exclusive social effects, and can empower or disempower people
standard.prior_knowledge: Students recognise how language empowers relationships and roles (AC9E9LA01). They have not yet analysed the inclusive/exclusive social effects of language — how it can empower or disempower people through alignment, inclusion and marginalisation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how language can have inclusive and exclusive social effects, and can empower or disempower people.

nodes.label: Alignment and distancing devices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language devices that seek to align or distance the listener/reader, including inclusive pronouns and assumptive phrases.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two alignment devices (e.g. ‘of course’, ‘we’) in a provided text and explain the intended effect on the audience.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain a range of alignment and distancing devices across print and multimodal texts, explaining how each positions the audience as insider or outsider.
wider: Analyse alignment devices across texts from different political or cultural contexts, comparing how ‘we’ and ‘you’ function differently in each
Examine how digital texts (social media posts, comment threads) use alignment language to construct in-group identity
Investigate how First Nations Australian speakers or writers use pronoun and alignment strategies in advocacy or community contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to identify language that references shared assumptions — a concept built on understanding how alignment devices position readers as insiders or outsiders. Without this, shared assumption analysis has no linguistic basis.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly assume alignment is always intentional and positive; encountering texts where alignment devices are used to exclude or manipulate broadens understanding of how these devices function across contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Alignment devices appear across a rich range of text types and cultural contexts — political speech, advertising, social media — offering genuine width in how they function differently for different audiences.
success_criteria: Identifies specific language devices (pronoun choices, assumptive phrases) that seek to align or distance an audience
Explains the intended social effect of at least one alignment device on a specified audience

nodes.label: Shared assumptions and cultural knowledge
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language that references shared assumptions and appeals to shared cultural knowledge, values and beliefs, and explain its inclusive or exclusive effect.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of language appealing to shared cultural knowledge in a provided text and explain who is included and who may be excluded.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how texts use references to shared cultural knowledge, values and beliefs to construct insider and outsider positions, across at least two different text contexts.
wider: Compare how texts targeting different cultural communities deploy different shared knowledge assumptions, examining what is taken for granted in each
Analyse examples where assumed shared knowledge marginalises particular groups — such as gendered or culturally specific references in media texts
Examine how First Nations Australian community communications draw on shared cultural knowledge to create solidarity and speak past mainstream gatekeeping
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to analyse how language empowers or disempowers people — a move that depends on understanding how shared assumption and exclusion operate. Students who cannot identify assumed cultural knowledge will miss the mechanism through which disempowerment occurs.

response_modes.reason: The inference required — identifying what is assumed rather than stated — needs explicit scaffolding for most students; the reasoning move from ‘what the text says’ to ‘what the text assumes’ is the core challenge here.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Texts that assume shared cultural knowledge are rich sites for examining how language constructs community and otherness — comparative work across cultural groups offers meaningful depth.
success_criteria: Identifies language that references or assumes shared cultural knowledge or values
Explains the inclusive effect on one audience group and the potentially exclusive effect on another

nodes.label: Empowerment and disempowerment through language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can understand how language choices can empower or disempower people, identifying examples of marginalising or inclusive language and explaining their social effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of language that is inclusive or marginalising in a provided text and explain the social effect on the people named or referenced.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how language in a range of texts empowers or disempowers people, considering how naming, labelling and inclusion/exclusion choices shape social effects across different contexts.
wider: Compare how empowering and disempowering language has been used historically and currently in relation to the same group — e.g. changing language around disability, First Nations identity, or gender
Examine political or media texts to trace how language choices have been used to disempower particular groups, and evaluate the social consequences
Analyse how communities have reclaimed previously marginalising language as an act of empowerment

response_modes.reason: Whether language is empowering or disempowering is highly context-dependent; students need to encounter multiple contexts to understand that the same word or phrase can have opposite effects depending on who uses it and in what setting.

This node integrates the alignment devices and shared assumptions from nodes 1–2 with broader social analysis — students coordinate their linguistic analysis with awareness of power and social context.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The social and historical range of contexts where language empowers or disempowers is extensive — First Nations reclamation, disability language, gender-inclusive language — offering rich comparative work.
success_criteria: Identifies specific language that empowers or disempowers people in a given text
Explains the social effect of the language choice on the people named or referenced, with reference to context
